subject: english-language

moments.title: The Social Differentiation of English in Norwich
moments.who: Peter Trudgill, University of East Anglia
moments.body: 1974: Trudgill's PhD work, based on a 1968 survey of Norwich, published. Variables include (ng) — pronounced /n/ or /ŋ/ in 'walking' — and others. Results show variation by class, age, gender and style. Working-class men use covert prestige forms (non-standard /n/); middle-class women use overt prestige.
moments.takeaway: Trudgill's study established that gender differences in linguistic variation are real and patterned — women generally using more standard forms than men of the same class.

moments.title: Sex, covert prestige and linguistic change
moments.body: Trudgill's 1972 paper introduces 'covert prestige' — non-standard forms valued within working-class male peer groups. The conflict between overt prestige (standard, middle-class) and covert prestige (non-standard, working-class male) is a major dynamic in sociolinguistic variation.
moments.takeaway: Covert prestige helps explain why non-standard varieties persist despite official disapproval — they carry social meaning users value.

moments.title: Sociolinguistic theory develops
moments.body: Lesley Milroy's Belfast work introduced social networks. Janet Holmes's New Zealand work on gender. Penelope Eckert's 'jocks and burnouts' study (1989) at a Detroit high school showed how identity drives variation. Trudgill's many books on sociolinguistics and dialectology made the field accessible.
moments.takeaway: Modern sociolinguistics is a major branch of academic English. A-level English Language studies its findings regularly.

now.title: Variation now
now.body: Modern variation studies use corpora, social media, and ethnography. Gender variation studies have become more nuanced (Robin Lakoff 1975's framework — 'women's language' — has been substantially critiqued and refined). Penelope Eckert's third-wave sociolinguistics emphasises identity construction over deterministic correlation.
now.open_questions: Why do women use standard forms more than men? Multiple competing explanations: social mobility, judgement of women's speech, identity work, network differences. The pattern is robust; the explanation contested.

reflection: A study in Norwich in the late 1960s established core findings of British sociolinguistics. The patterns Trudgill identified — class, gender, style — still organise how variation is studied. Sociolinguistics owes much of its modern shape to this work.
